Status of anonymous concerns submitted to the Faculty Senate - Senate President Preisser announced that this will now be a standing item on meeting agendas to allow the Executive Committee an opportunity to provide answers to questions asked anonymously.

CRCA Informational Report - Goals and Priorities for the Year - After noting the current membership of her committee and its subcommittee, Chair Buxton first reviewed the CRCA priorities during AY 25-26 which did not come to fruition and will carry over.
She then noted the committee’s goal for this year will be to 4

prioritize ‘low-hanging’ fruit, i.e. specific action items wherein the CRCA can exert meaningful influence and/or take steps to address directly.
This will include developing concrete proposals to tangibly improve URI research infrastructure and support.
The CRCA is positioned to be the voice for the entire research presence across the university and the committee is intent on finding actionable projects within their control to focus on this year.
Faculty with specific concerns were encouraged to reach out to Chair Buxton or other committee members.
It was also noted that the opening of a new round of competitive grants will be announced by the end of the calendar year, and all research active faculty, especially newer faculty, are encouraged to pursue these funding opportunities.
Past awardees and other qualified faculty who will not be applying this year are asked to assist in proposal review.
Subcommittee Chair Wei should be contacted by interested parties.
The CRCA and grants subcommittee reports were accepted. ii.

TAAC Informational Report - Goals and Priorities for the Year - Chair Romanow noted her committee ended last academic year with a ‘clean slate,’ having completed a number of projects and reviews.
They have thus set new priorities for AY 26-27, with interest areas emerging from concerns identified either by their own committee members or by FSEC.
Work will center around: examining the effectiveness and applicability of the ‘Hacking College Model’ which connects student interests with coursework, experiential learning, and careers with the goal of increased retention.
It is currently being piloted in some sections of URI 101.
Chair Romanow noted there is a new Advisory Council being led by the Director of Academic Advising Services and TAAC will have a representative involved.
Regarding admissions,the TAAC will continue to liaise with AVP Libutti’s office and keep the senate informed of any issues related to admissions standards and processes, and the university’s ability to recruit high-achieving students.
Chair Romanow’s report was accepted. iii.

Priorities for AY 26-27 will include: fostering collaboration with the DIversity Council and otherwise supporting DEI efforts, including collecting information on how faculty are addressing emergent challenges in that area; considering how service work is viewed and valued across the university, and assisting in a specific faculty initiative aimed at building institutional support for mid-career faculty.
Chair Kusz’s report was accepted. iv.

improving data interoperability (for example, across InfoEd, Grants, eCampus, Interfolio, Parking).
In terms of specific initiatives for AY 26/27, the committee would like to launch a survey on Responsible AI Usage for Research to better understand faculty needs, practices, habits, and ethics.

NEW BUSINESS - a.
FORUM - Discussion of College Liaisons - Pres.
Preisser prosented a draft proposal that would create a special committee of ‘College Liaisons.’ He briefly outlined the need for such a special committee and provided some background on how the idea emerged from the Executive Committee more than two years ago and how it has evolved since then.
The Committee members would have two main responsibilities, with that scope of work having been refined with the input of the college deans.
The primary tasks of the special committee will include providing a monthly written update regarding senate/university-level matters to all faculty in their college.
And secondly, liaisons represent their college at meetings of the Special Committee.
The committee will meet at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination.

These may include, but are not limited to, best practices in college-level faculty governance and fostering inter-college research or academic collaborations.
A number of faculty members responded to the proposal with questions and concerns.
Pres.
Preisser clarified that, as currently conceived, the initial iteration of the special committee of liaisons would involve senators volunteering for additional service commitments.
A show of hands revealed that sitting senators value the liaison role, as proposed, but would be more apt to serve on the special committee if that were their only senate committee obligation, rather than an additional assignment.
There were questions about the actual mechanics of how the new special committee would work and Pres.
Preisser noted that part of the value in creating the committee this year would be to see how it operates and how effective it will be at enacting its charge.
A benefit of convening a special committee is the ability to learn from its operations on the ground so that its success as a permanent committee, if so created, might be augmented by that experience.

It was noted that other opportunities for faculty from across colleges to convene conversations around shared interest in governance are severely limited and the Liaisons Committee could fill that void.
Pres.
Preisser and others emphasized that the committee would not be a redundancy: although all senators are expected to act as a conduit between their colleges and the senate, the liaison role would formalize two-way communications in a way that has not been done in the past.
President Preisser noted the feedback from this forum will be used to refine a formal proposal for introduction at a future meeting. 10.

Capital Improvement Plan FY22‐FY26 Presentation to the Finance and Facilities Committee October 23, 2020

What is the Capital Improvement Plan? • 5 Year plan that shows projects that have a total project cost of greater than $1 Million • It is a rolling plan that is submitted annually as a request to the state, typically on July 1st. Who Approves the Capital Improvement Plan? There are 5 levels of approval. They are: 1. University of Rhode Island ‐ Facilities Committee (April & May) 2. University of Rhode Island ‐ Senior Leadership (May & June) 3. University of Rhode Island ‐ Board of Trustees (June) 4. Executive Branch 1. Analysis performed and Recommendations made by the Office of Management and Budget (July‐December) 2. Final Approval by Governor’s Office (Third week of January) 5. Legislative Branch 1. Analysis performed and Recommendations made by both the House and Senate Fiscal Offices (January – June) 2. Final Plan approved as part of the RI Budget Appropriations Bill (June) How is a project added to the Capital Improvement Plan? • In order to receive consideration, all projects must be submitted on the Capital Improvement Request form by a member of the Senior Leadership to the URI Office of Planning & Real Estate Development • Most projects will have an advanced planning study performed prior to inclusion in the Capital Improvement plan to determine program, siting, massing, and, total expected project cost
What does the Capital Improvement Plan cover? The University of Rhode Island’s Board of Trustees is responsible for about 25% of the State’s total real estate portfolio.
